items_missed: No agenda statement and no agenda-level 'sound good?'. The call opened 'Hello, this is Hector with Einstein movie. How may I help you?' and went straight to the date question. The customer was never told what the call would cover or that it takes 10-15 minutes. (The one 'Does that sound good?' in the call is about the 1:30 slot, not the agenda.)
Never asked 'How are you today?' or any warm-up before diving into 'do you have a date in mind for your move'.
Never asked for the customer's name. He backed into it off the email spelling ('Mary.Belton BEL T, O. N 87 @yahoo.com') and only used it once, near the end, as 'miss Mary'.

SAVE YOUR ASS SECTION NEVER HAPPENED — 0/10, and it was the single clearest opportunity on the call. The customer said outright 'that's gonna be like a, like the morning of all the you know throwing should just wherever kind of thing and just here take it' and later 'me and my mom are going to do the whole throw everything together stuff that morning'. Hector's response was to pad the estimate ('I'll kind of lean a little bit more on the higher end') instead of coaching prep. No prep-equals-lower-bill framing, no consolidation examples, no 'take a carload' tip — even though she volunteered 'I would take that back with me' about the cube shelf, handing him the carload opening.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned. He described a day-of ETA call instead — 'our movers they do give you a call from their personal phones whenever they're headed your direction' — which is not the Meet Your Mover email with the mover's photo and info a few days ahead.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener. The rate arrived at the tail of one very long uninterrupted block rather than being framed up front.
Incomplete what's-included list. He covered padded blankets, shrink wrap, disassembly/reassembly and No Worries, but never named gas, truck, taxes, insurance, bands, or tools.

No full 'no hidden fees' pitch — no credit card fees, no transportation fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees. He got partway with 'no need to worry about, you know, particular fee for a specific task' and the free-travel-zone note, but never ran the differentiator.

Packing services never offered or priced, on a call where the customer twice described packing as an unmanaged morning-of scramble with an unknown box count. Same hourly rate plus materials was never stated. This is lost revenue and a direct cause of the estimate risk he then padded for.
Ecobox never mentioned despite an unknown box count and a customer with no boxes gathered — 'I'm not quite sure' on box count.
No storage question and no additional-stops question.

Origin stairs/floors never asked. He carefully covered the apartment ('what floor is it gonna be on?', 'elevator access or are there stairs nearby?') but never asked about steps, porch, or driveway at the Liberty Hill house.

Additional rooms never swept. He asked bedrooms, living room, appliances and TVs, but never garage, shed, attic, storage unit, patio, or balcony — on a rural county-road property where a garage or shed is likely.

Never asked the moving-stressor question. No version of 'is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?' — and she surfaced real anxiety twice (missing the movers' call, and getting done in time to pick up her daughter).
Clock start never explained. The 2.5-hour minimum and 15-minute prorated increments were both covered well, but he never said the clock starts on-site when the contract opens.

No typical time range for the home size. He gave a hard 4.25 hours built from segments (2 hours load, 45 minutes drive, 1.5 hours unload) but never anchored it to what a move like this usually runs, so the customer has a point estimate with no band around it.

Stairs never explained as a time variable. He learned the unit is a second-floor walk-up ('it's just like a set of stairs to go up to the second floor') and priced it silently instead of telling her stairs add time to the unload.

No BOLDED-details framing for the confirmation email and no 'reply with any corrections'. He said only 'I'll go ahead and send you the confirmation email to mary.Belton. 87 @yahoo.com' — so the details he keyed in, including the guessed 1,000 sqft and the 'TV Number two question mark', are never put back in front of her to verify.

No 'any other questions before I let you go?' check in the call. He went from the booking confirmation straight into the farewell; the invitation to ask questions was a call-us-later version, 'give us a shout and ask for me'.
Hours of operation and a way to reach the company never given — no number, no hours, just 'ask for me'.
60 cents per pound baseline never mentioned alongside the $2,000 No Worries coverage, so the insurance explanation is missing its comparison point.
Customer's name used once. 'Miss Mary' at the close is the only instance — short of the 3+ standard.

Let a day-of-week error stand. The customer said 'do you have an opening for like, noon? Like Friday at noon?' while the agreed date was Wednesday September 9. He answered 'Sure. I can put it for noon, specifically' and never corrected 'Friday'. He did re-confirm 'Wednesday September 9th for a start time of noon ish' at the end, but the mismatch was never named, so she may still be holding Friday in her head.
top_strength: The estimate build was the best thing on this call and it is genuinely coachable-to-others work. Hector priced the job out loud, phase by phase, instead of dropping a number: he set the load at 'pretty much around two hours like even if it is like a higher box counts like your furniture is pretty mini minimal', the drive at 45 minutes, the unload at 'about an hour and a half', then rolled it to '4.25' hours at '$96 per mover per hour' times two movers and one truck for 'around $800'. His drive-time reasoning was better than most reps ever get to: 'according to what the Google ETA is that tends to be a little optimistic compared to how fast our larger trucks can go so to that end is like I am going to bake in perhaps about like ten to fifteen minutes of extra time just to allow for wiggle room for traffic as well.' He was also excellent on proactive FAQs and on trust-building differentiators he did reach: the TV power-cord instruction ('we also ask that you keep the power cord with it. That way we could test it before and after we move it'), the in-house repair team ('we have our own in-house team so that way it's not like outsource to a third party company and hopes that it's forgotten kind of thing'), the spam-caller aside that landed as real rapport, and the On-Time Guarantee delivered with the actual mechanic and a reason to believe it: 'if we arrive after when we start deducting from the overall cost of your move starting with $50... that's a common problem in the moving industries like some people are just left hanging.' The customer closed the call with 'thank you so much Hector. I appreciate your help with all this' — earned.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, and it is worth more than everything else combined on this call: the customer told Hector twice that she was going to pack morning-of, and he answered by padding the estimate instead of running the Save Your Ass speech. When she said 'that's gonna be like the morning of all the you know throwing should just wherever kind of thing and just here take it', the line he needed was: 'Mary, let me save you some money here — the clock runs while we pack and consolidate, so anything you can box up before Wednesday comes straight off your bill. Get your daughter's toys into bins, empty the loose stuff out of the dresser drawers, take the wall photos down, and stage it all by the front door. And anything small and fragile — take a carload yourself the night before. Do that and this could land closer to three and a half hours than four and a quarter. Does that make sense?' That one speech does three things at once: it shortens the move, it lands the differentiator he skipped, and it fixes the estimate-accuracy exposure he created by leaning conservative on an unknown box count. Second priority: offer packing services in the same breath — she is describing a job that needs them, she was never told they exist, and the price is the same hourly rate plus materials. Third: Meet Your Mover. He had the perfect setup when she worried about missing the movers' call ('if I'm like trying to get stuff together I hopefully won't miss it'), and instead of 'you'll also get a Meet Your Mover email a few days before with your mover's photo and info, so you'll know exactly who's coming', he stayed on the day-of call. Business risks to close in EMMA today: (1) The arrival window contradicts the reason she wanted an afternoon slot. She asked for after 12 specifically because she and her mom are packing that morning, and he then told her a noon booking means an 11:00-to-1:00 window. If the crew shows at 11 she is not ready and the clock starts anyway — either move the booking later or set the expectation explicitly that they will not knock before noon. (2) She said 'Friday at noon' and the job is booked Wednesday September 9; he never corrected it out loud. Put the day, date and window in the confirmation email in bold and ask her to reply to confirm. (3) The record carries two guesses that need verifying — a 1,000 sqft figure he supplied himself ('generally a two bedroom will be somewhere along the lines of around a thousand square feet') and a 'TV Number two question mark' — plus an unknown box count and no origin-stairs data on a rural property. (4) There is an unexplained '$116 for the month' in the transcript immediately after the $800 estimate, and her very next line was 'Do I pay that right now?' — confirm what that figure was and whether she left the call with the wrong number in her head.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and affirming with real empathy markers — 'Fantastic', 'Of course', 'no worries', the spam-caller aside, and a genuine accommodation of her school-pickup timing ('Understood, no worries. Yeah, yeah, I totally get you') — held back from a 5 by heavy verbal filler ('gotcha, gotcha', 'cool, cool, cool') and one long monologue where he delivered the entire estimate and price without pausing for her.
audio_review_reason: Two spots text cannot settle. First, the estimate-and-pricing delivery is one enormous uninterrupted block against roughly fourteen consecutive 'Mm-hmm' lines from the customer, so it is impossible to tell from the transcript whether she was tracking the numbers or being talked at. Second, an unexplained '$116 for the month' appears immediately after the $800 total with no surrounding context, and her next line is 'Do I pay that right now, or do I pay that after in case it takes less time?' — the audio is needed to establish what that figure was and what she believes she is paying.
